subject: English
stem: The nation was gaining ground at this time as the acceptable and \(\underline{\text{legible}}\) idiom of collective political demands.
solution: The block asks for the word opposite in meaning to the underlined one. Legible describes something that can be made out and understood. Intelligible, decipherable and readable all restate that same idea, so none of them can be its opposite. Incomprehensible means impossible to understand, which reverses it exactly. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Among its distinctive features is a \(\underline{\text{conflation}}\) between land, a national(ised) language, and a people.
solution: The block asks for the opposite of the underlined word. Conflation names the running together of two separate things into one. Amalgamation and meld both name that same merging, and an emulsion is likewise two substances held together as a single mixture, so all three sit on the same side as the underlined word. By contrast, a constituent is one component of a whole, an element kept distinct rather than fused, so it alone points the other way. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Weak item: (a) amalgamation, (b) meld and (d) emulsion are all synonyms of "conflation"; the key (c) "constituent" is right only by elimination, being a component part rather than a true opposite of a merging.

subject: English
stem: The partners maintained an \(\underline{\text{amicable}}\) relation­ ship after selling the business.
solution: Amicable means friendly and good-natured. Amiable, gracious and mellow all repeat that sense in different registers. Surly means bad-tempered and unfriendly, which is the reverse of an amicable relationship. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: For clinicians under the occupation, whose patients were dying from hunger, this presented an ethical \(\underline{\text{quandary}}\) and a personal dilemma.
solution: Quandary names the state of not knowing which course to take. The sentence itself glosses it with the words a personal dilemma, so quagmire and predicament, which both name a difficult fix, are near synonyms and cannot be the opposite. Tranquility names calm, which is a different axis altogether. The reverse of not knowing what to do is knowing, that is certainty. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: The CEO has been praised for his \(\underline{\text{adroit}}\) management of the company's financial recovery.
solution: Adroit means skilful and deft in handling a matter. Skillful and dexterous simply restate it, and ambidextrous names a related manual facility rather than its reverse. Gauche means clumsy and tactless, and the pair is exact even in origin, since adroit comes from the French for right-handed and gauche from the French for left-handed. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: The earthquake destroyed thousands of people’s lives but I was struck by the incredible \(\underline{\text{resilience}}\) of the survivors I met.
solution: Resilience is the capacity to absorb a shock and recover from it. Potency and tenacity are strengths of the same family, and obstinate is not even a noun and so cannot replace it. Weakness is the plain reverse of that capacity to withstand and bounce back. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: This process taught me the importance of being a \(\underline{\text{ruthless}}\) editor. I learnt that if a piece of information can be deleted without impacting the narrative flow, then it didn't belong there.
solution: Ruthless means showing no pity, which is why the sentence uses it of an editor who deletes without hesitation. Callous, meaning hardened and unfeeling, is its close synonym and is the trap set here. Boorish means rude and ill-mannered and acrimonious means bitter in tone, and neither of those reverses pitilessness. Compassionate, full of pity for others, does. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: With little access to medical care, many of them \(\underline{\text{succumbed}}\) to exhaustion, starvation and disease.
solution: To succumb to something is to stop resisting it and give way to it, so those who succumbed to exhaustion, starvation and disease were overcome by them and gave in. Capitulate carries exactly that sense of ceasing to resist and yielding to a force one can no longer withstand. Of the others, to battle is the opposite, since it means to go on resisting; defeated will not fit either the sense or the grammar, because a person is defeated by a hardship and never defeated to it, whereas the sentence has succumbed to; and sonorous, meaning deep and resonant in sound, has nothing to do with the meaning at all. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: The section instruction does not survive in the stem, so the direction has to be inferred from the option block, and the block contains BOTH a synonym and an opposite, which is the risk here. 'Succumb to' means to stop resisting and give way to, so 'capitulate' is the exact synonym; 'battle' is its opposite. I read this as a nearest-meaning item, because 'capitulate' is a textbook-perfect synonym while 'battle' is only a loose opposite (the natural antonyms would be 'resisted' or 'overcame'), and because the sister rows in this series that share this shape, a single underlined word in a full sentence with four meanings offered, are synonym items. 'Defeated' fails on grammar as well as sense, since one is defeated BY a thing, never defeated TO it, whereas the sentence has 'succumbed to'; 'sonorous' is unrelated. FLAG for a human: if the printed section heading turns out to be Antonyms, the answer is 'battle' instead.]

subject: English
stem: A \(\underline{\text{frugal}}\) lifestyle doesn’t have to mean a deprived lifestyle.
solution: Frugal means careful and sparing with money. Parsimony and niggardly both describe that same sparingness, if anything more severely, and thrifty is its everyday synonym. By contrast, a spendthrift lifestyle is one of wasteful spending, the reverse of sparing. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: A \(\underline{\text{sedentary}}\) lifestyle could increase your levels of exhaustion.
solution: Sedentary describes a life spent sitting still and taking little exercise. Dormant, apathetic and somnambulant all keep to that same idea of inactivity or sluggishness. Animated means lively and full of movement, which reverses it. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Recently, 23 of Watauga’s best math students met virtually to test their \(\underline{\text{mettle}}\) against their peers in the annual Math Counts competition.
solution: This block asks for the word closest in meaning to the underlined one. Mettle is the quality or ability a person shows when put to the test. The sentence sets the students against their peers in a competition, so what is being measured is the standard they reach relative to others, that is their caliber. Placidity means calmness, which is not what a contest measures, and adore is a verb and cannot stand in for a noun. Matches option A.
reviewNote: (b) "resolution" is a defensible second reading of "mettle" (resolve); the key (a) "caliber" fits the competition context (quality / ability) better.

subject: English
stem: Since the \(\underline{\text{callow}}\) baker was new to cake deco­ rating, she did not know how to properly frost the multi-layer cake.
solution: Callow describes someone not yet matured by experience, and the standard dictionary gloss of the word is simply immature. The sentence supplies the evidence by saying the baker was new to cake decorating. Puerile and childish both mean silly in the manner of a child, which is a judgement on behaviour rather than on inexperience, and seasoned means experienced and is the opposite. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Weak item: (a) puerile and (b) childish are also synonyms of "callow"; the key (c) "immature" is the neutral dictionary synonym while the other two carry a "silly" connotation. (d) "seasoned" is the antonym.

subject: English
stem: The magazine article provided ideas for activities designed to shake off the \(\underline{\text{torpor}}\) of a rainy day.
solution: Torpor is a noun meaning sluggishness and want of energy. Naive, dispassionate and fervent are all adjectives and cannot replace a noun in the sentence, and fervent, meaning passionate, would in any case reverse the sense. Tepidity is the noun for lukewarmness and lack of enthusiasm, which is the flatness a rainy day produces. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: The \(\underline{\text{incumbents}}\) for the Fayetteville and Rogers school boards all secured their seats for another term.
solution: An incumbent is the person currently holding an office, and the sentence confirms it by saying they secured their seats for another term. An officeholder is exactly that. An entrant is someone newly coming in, which is the opposite of a sitting holder and is the trap. Vehemence means forcefulness of feeling and azure is a shade of blue. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: The pole vaulter reached the \(\underline{\text{apogee}}\) of height in the competition, catapulting him into first place.
solution: The apogee is the highest point reached, and apex names that same summit. Heyday is a peak in time, a period of greatest success, whereas the sentence is measuring height in a vault and not a stretch of years. Inane means silly and accommodate is a verb. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: I attempted to \(\underline{\text{aggrandize}}\) the CEO’s high status in the company to sweet talk him into signing off on the deal.
solution: To aggrandize someone is to build up their power, wealth or importance, that is to elevate their standing. Abase means to lower or humiliate and is the opposite. Perigee, the point of nearest approach, is offered as a false pair for apogee, and an aeon is a vast stretch of time. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Seven \(\underline{\text{plenteous}}\) years brought enough food to feed the people during the famine.
solution: Plenteous means existing in great quantity, and the sentence confirms it by saying those years brought enough food to feed the people through a famine. Abundant carries precisely that sense. Scarcity is its opposite and niggardly means stingy. Fecund means fertile or prolific, which describes a cause of plenty rather than plenty itself. Matches option C.
reviewNote: (d) "fecund" (fertile / productive) is a near-miss; the key (c) "abundant" is the direct synonym of "plenteous".

subject: English
stem: The \(\underline{\text{indictments}}\) against the company and its chief financial officer, Allen Weisselberg, will remain sealed until Thursday.
solution: An indictment is a formal charge brought against someone before a court, which is why these ones can be sealed until a named day. An arraignment is that same formal charging. Exoneration and praise both clear or commend rather than accuse, and rhythm is unrelated. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: The student was \(\underline{\text{procrastinating}}\) writing the report; however, the tutor provided the needed guidance and motivation.
solution: Procrastinating is a verb form, and of the four choices only loiter is a verb, since diatonic and diminutive are adjectives and lackadaisically is an adverb. Loiter also carries the required sense of hanging back and putting off the next move. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Sloppy option set: the underlined word is a present participle while (c) "loiter" is a bare infinitive and (d) "lackadaisically" is an adverb. (c) is nonetheless the only semantically plausible option.

subject: English
stem: The facts of the unsolved mystery were intriguing, but the author’s conclusion was \(\underline{\text{facile}}\).
solution: Facile describes something reached too easily, and the sentence sets it against facts that were intriguing, so the complaint is that the conclusion was shallow and undemanding. Simple carries that sense of easy and uncomplicated. Arduous, meaning laborious, is the opposite, while torrid means scorching and dally is a verb. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: The plot of the story thickens when the main character’s ____________ turns out to be a wanted criminal.
solution: The blank is the subject of turns out to be, so it must be a noun, which rules out lugubrious, lovelorn and woeful, all adjectives. The word doppelganger names a person's exact double, and a double turning out to be a wanted criminal is precisely the twist that would thicken a plot. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: “I’m not willing to___________ my friendship with Camille by lying to her,” said Luis.
solution: The blank follows willing to, so it needs the base form of a verb, which rules out the adjectives dismayed and distraught. Jeopardize means to put at risk, and lying to a friend is exactly what would put a friendship at risk. To wriggle is to twist the body about and cannot take friendship as its object. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Any insect unlucky enough to land on the mouth-like leaves of an Australian pitcher plant will meet a _________ end.
solution: The phrase a grisly end means a gruesome one, which is what a carnivorous pitcher plant gives the insect that lands on it. Grizzly, the near-identical word set beside it as a trap, means greyish and names a species of bear; it never describes a death. Teary-eyed and mewling describe the look or sound of distress rather than the manner of an end. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: A number of serious disorders, such as sickle cell anemia and Huntington’s disease are caused by genetic________.
solution: The blank names what causes the disorders, so it must be a departure from the normal genetic pattern. An anomaly is exactly such an irregularity, and genetic anomalies is the standard phrase. Eccentricity is oddity of personal behaviour, ebullience is high spirits, and ecclesiastics are clergymen. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: At an early age, when grammar school teachers were struggling to _________ the lesson that effort was the main key to success in school.
solution: The teachers are trying to fix a lesson in their pupils' minds. To inculcate is to instil an idea by persistent teaching, which is that action exactly. Evade means to avoid, the reverse of what a teacher does with a lesson, while dubious and quaint are adjectives and cannot follow struggling to. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Printed stem is a sentence fragment - the subordinate clause "At an early age, when grammar school teachers were struggling to ___ the lesson that effort was the main key to success in school." has no main clause. Source defect; not answer-affecting.

subject: English
stem: She gave him her most_________ smile and stepped out of the hallway.
solution: The blank sits inside the superlative her most blank smile, so it needs an adjective naming an attractive quality that a person could deliberately turn on. Fetching means charming or appealing and collocates naturally with smile. Irritated and confused describe an involuntary state rather than something one gives to another, and a most surprising smile does not fit a deliberate parting gesture. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: It’s an _________ cloud, a phenomenon occur­ ring right in our own atmosphere.
solution: The sentence calls the cloud a phenomenon occurring in our own atmosphere, so the blank must name what makes it remarkable. Iridescence is the shimmering play of rainbow colour seen in thin cloud, and an iridescent cloud is the recognised name for that effect. Azure means simply blue, which is unremarkable in the sky and would not be called a phenomenon, while seaweed and pandemic have nothing to do with clouds. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Famed actor Phylicia Rashad is returning to her _____ as the new dean of the Howard University College of Fine Arts.
solution: One returns to the institution where one studied, and the name for that institution is one's alma mater. Alumni is the plural word for the graduates themselves and not for the college, so a person cannot return to her alumni. Pagan and baroque have nothing to do with schooling. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: As people grow older, they begin to _______ on the uncertainty of life.
solution: The blank takes the preposition on and must mean to turn something over in the mind. To ruminate on a subject is exactly that. Vivid is an adjective, daunt means to intimidate and needs a person as its object rather than the preposition on, and a fiasco is a noun. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: He seemed burdened with _________ thoughts and dark visions as he wrestled with his pursuing demons.
solution: The thoughts are paired with dark visions and pursuing demons, so the blank must strike the same gloomy note. Melancholic means sorrowful and dejected. Heterodox means unorthodox in belief, sonorous describes a deep rich sound, and wacky means eccentrically funny, none of which fits the darkness of the sentence. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: Out of the woods
solution: In this idiom the woods stand for danger or difficulty and not for actual trees, so being out of them means being past the point of danger. Out of the forest is the literal reading the idiom is precisely not asking for, and out of control reverses the sense of safety altogether. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Call a spade a spade
optC: In a state where one does not know what to do
optD: To tackle a problem in a bold and direct fashion
solution: To call a spade a spade is to name a thing plainly by its proper name without softening it, so the idiom describes a manner of speaking: blunt and direct. Tackling a problem in a bold and direct fashion belongs to a different idiom, taking the bull by the horns; it describes action rather than speech, and it is the trap here because it repeats the words bold and direct. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: At daggers drawn
optB: To tackle a problem in a bold and direct fashion
optD: Have a secret plan in reserve
solution: Daggers drawn is the moment before a fight, with the weapons already out of their sheaths, so two people at daggers drawn are in open and bitter enmity. Bitterly hostile states that. Keeping one at a distance describes mere coolness and falls well short of drawn weapons. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Bark up the wrong tree
optA: Confess – especially when a person has done a wrong thing
optC: Waste one’s efforts by pursuing the wrong thing or path
solution: The image is of a hound baying at the foot of a tree the quarry never climbed. The effort is genuine but it is aimed at the wrong place, which is to waste one's efforts by pursuing the wrong thing or path. Accusing or denouncing a person belongs to a different phrase and misses the point, since the one barking is mistaken rather than aggressive. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: At one’s wit's end
solution: Wit here means one's power of thinking, so to be at the end of it is to have run out of ideas and no longer know what to do. Completely puzzled or perplexed states that condition. Tired and without hope describe fatigue and despair, which are different states and not a loss of ideas. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Have a card up one’s sleeve
optA: Do or say the exact thing
optD: Have a secret plan in reserve
solution: The image is of a card player concealing a playing card in his sleeve, an advantage held back until the moment it is needed. That is to have a secret plan in reserve. Making a supreme effort and acting foolishly have nothing to do with a concealed advantage. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Cock and bull story
optB: Made up story that one should not believe
solution: A cock and bull story is a far-fetched, invented tale offered as an excuse or an explanation and not worth believing, as in 'He turned up two hours late with some cock and bull story about his train being hijacked.' The phrase comes from the tall tales that were traded at old coaching inns. So it means a made up story that one should not believe. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: Take a leaf out of one’s book
solution: To take a leaf out of someone's book is to copy the way that person does something, because their way is working, as in 'You should take a leaf out of your sister's book and start revising a month before the exam.' The image behind it is that of tearing a page, a leaf, out of another person's book and using it as your own. So the phrase means to imitate one. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Bury the hatchet
optC: End the quarrel and make peace
optD: Put or do things in the wrong order Idioms & phrases Vocabulary
solution: Among the Native American tribes the ceremonial burying of a tomahawk was the sign that fighting between two groups had stopped. From this, to bury the hatchet means to settle a quarrel and become friends again, as in 'The two brothers finally buried the hatchet after ten years of not speaking.' The literal picture of putting a weapon underground tempts a reader towards 'destroy in the early stage', but that idea belongs to a different phrase, to nip something in the bud. Matches option C.
